title: The Second Lincoln-Douglas Debate at Freeport, Illinois (August 27, 1858)
context: Authentic historical reconstruction of the second joint senatorial debate between Republican challenger Abraham Lincoln and Democratic incumbent Senator Stephen A. Douglas before 15,000 spectators at Freeport, Illinois, on August 27, 1858, opened and presided over by Freeport Chairman Hon. Thomas J. Turner. Tracks Lincoln's replies to Douglas's Ottawa interrogatories, Lincoln's pivotal four Freeport Questions targeting the contradiction between popular sovereignty and Dred Scott v. Sandford, Douglas's formulation of the 'Freeport Doctrine' on local police regulations and unfriendly legislation, the moral and constitutional divide over slavery expansion, and Lincoln's closing rejoinder.

metadata.historical_outcome: Douglas articulated the Freeport Doctrine, narrowly retaining his Illinois Senate seat in 1858 while fatally fracturing the national Democratic Party ahead of the 1860 presidential election.

turns.speaker: Thomas J. Turner
turns.text: Citizens of Stephenson County and fellow residents of Illinois, as chairman of the committee of arrangements here in Freeport, I call this immense assembly to order. Under the agreed terms of the joint senatorial canvass, the Honorable Abraham Lincoln will open the debate for one hour, Senator Stephen A. Douglas will follow for an hour and a half, and Mr. Lincoln will close with a half-hour rejoinder. Let every gentleman on both sides preserve quiet order so all fifteen thousand voices may hear these great constitutional questions argued fairly.

turns.speaker: Abraham Lincoln
turns.text: Ladies and gentlemen, on Saturday last at Ottawa, Senator Douglas took the liberty of putting seven specific interrogatories to me, challenging me to answer whether I stand pledged to repeal the Fugitive Slave Law, oppose the admission of new slave states, or abolish slavery in the District of Columbia. I have come to Freeport today resolved to answer every single one of those seven questions plainly, candidly, and without equivocation, and then I shall place four equally direct questions before Senator Douglas for his answer to the people of Illinois.

turns.speaker: Abraham Lincoln
turns.text: First, I do not now, nor ever did, stand pledged against the unconditional repeal of the Fugitive Slave Law; though I believe the Southern people are entitled under the Constitution to a fugitive slave law, the existing statute might be framed with better safeguards so free men are not seized without due process. Second, I am not pledged against the admission of any more slave states into the Union if slavery has already been established therein by the people prior to application, though I should be exceedingly sorry ever to be put in a position of having to pass upon that question—because I firmly believe that if slavery is kept out of the territories, no new slave state will ever seek admission. Third, I am not pledged to abolish slavery in the District of Columbia, though I believe Congress possesses the constitutional power to do so on condition of compensation and the consent of its inhabitants. Above all, I stand pledged against the extension of slavery into any federal territory where it does not now exist.

turns.speaker: Stephen A. Douglas
turns.text: I am delighted that I have at last succeeded in bringing Mr. Lincoln to the confessional box on a portion of the platform adopted by his Black Republican abolitionist allies in 1854. Yet notice how delicately he qualifies his answers here in Northern Illinois while refusing to declare whether he would admit Kansas as a slave state even if her people should desire it. The Democratic principle of popular sovereignty rests on the eternal right of self-government: let the people of every territory and state regulate their own domestic institutions, including slavery, in their own way, subject only to the Constitution of the United States.

turns.speaker: Thomas J. Turner
turns.text: Order in the crowd, please. Mr. Lincoln is proceeding to the second portion of his opening address, propounding four formal interrogatories to Senator Douglas regarding Kansas, territorial exclusion, the Dred Scott decision, and territorial expansion.

turns.speaker: Abraham Lincoln
turns.text: Now, gentlemen, having answered every question Senator Douglas asked me at Ottawa, I propose to give him an opportunity to answer four questions of mine. First: If the people of Kansas shall, by means entirely unobjectionable in all other respects, adopt a State Constitution, and ask admission into the Union under it, before they have the requisite number of inhabitants according to the English Bill—some ninety-three thousand—will you vote to admit them?

turns.speaker: Abraham Lincoln
turns.text: Second—and I ask the closest attention of every citizen to this question: Can the people of a United States Territory, in any lawful way, against the wish of any citizen of the United States, exclude slavery from its limits prior to the formation of a State Constitution? Third: If the Supreme Court of the United States shall decide that States cannot exclude slavery from their limits, are you in favor of acquiescing in, adopting, and following such decision as a rule of political action? Fourth: Are you in favor of acquiring additional territory, in disregard of how such acquisition may affect the nation on the slavery question?

turns.speaker: Stephen A. Douglas
turns.text: Mr. Lincoln's second question is not new to me; I have answered it a hundred times from the stump in Illinois and on the floor of the United States Senate, and I have no hesitation in answering it here at Freeport before friends and political foes alike. Yet let me remind the audience that Mr. Lincoln seeks to trap popular sovereignty between the Kansas-Nebraska Act and Chief Justice Taney's Dred Scott opinion, pretending that a territorial legislature cannot exercise self-government without violating the Supreme Court.

turns.speaker: Thomas J. Turner
turns.text: Mr. Lincoln's opening hour has concluded. Under the joint agreement, Senator Stephen A. Douglas now takes the platform for ninety minutes to deliver his reply and expound his doctrine on territorial legislatures and the Supreme Court.

turns.speaker: Stephen A. Douglas
turns.text: First, as to Kansas, I hold it to be a sound rule of universal application that a people ought to have enough population to constitute a state before claiming representation in the Senate, and that rule applies equally to free states and slave states alike. Second, Mr. Lincoln asks me whether the people of a Territory can, in any lawful way, exclude slavery from their limits prior to the formation of a State Constitution. I answer emphatically, as I have always done, that in my opinion the people of a Territory can, by lawful means, exclude slavery from their limits prior to the formation of a State Constitution!

turns.speaker: Stephen A. Douglas
turns.text: Mr. Lincoln has heard me answer this again and again. It matters not what way the Supreme Court may hereafter decide as to the abstract question whether slavery may or may not go into a Territory under the Constitution; the people have the lawful means to introduce it or exclude it as they please, for the reason that slavery cannot exist a day or an hour anywhere, unless it is supported by local police regulations! Those police regulations can only be established by the local legislature, and if the people are opposed to slavery, they will elect representatives to that body who will by unfriendly legislation effectually prevent the introduction of it into their midst. If, on the contrary, they are for it, their legislation will favor its extension. Hence, no matter what the decision of the Supreme Court may be on that abstract question, still the right of the people to make a slave Territory or a free Territory is perfect and complete under the Nebraska Bill.

turns.speaker: Stephen A. Douglas
turns.text: Third, as to whether the Supreme Court could ever decide that a sovereign State cannot exclude slavery, I regard that as an insult to the Court—a political imputation fabricated by Mr. Lincoln to alarm Northern voters after Chief Justice Taney ruled that Congress lacks power to prohibit slavery in the federal territories. Fourth, whenever it becomes necessary in our growth and progress to acquire more territory, I am in favor of it, without reference to the question of slavery, trusting the people who settle there to govern themselves under popular sovereignty.

turns.speaker: Abraham Lincoln
turns.text: Mark well what Senator Douglas has just declared! He tells us that even though the Supreme Court in Dred Scott ruled that the Constitution protects a master's right to carry his slave property into any federal territory, the territorial legislature may nonetheless starve that constitutional right out of existence through 'unfriendly legislation' and the withholding of local police regulations. What is this Freeport Doctrine? If the Constitution actually guarantees the right of property in slaves in a territory, how can a subordinate territorial legislature lawfully pass unfriendly laws to destroy a right guaranteed by the supreme law of the land? Judge Douglas either admits Dred Scott is wrong as a rule of territorial law, or he invites territorial legislatures to nullify a constitutional right he claims is sacred!

turns.speaker: Stephen A. Douglas
turns.text: Mr. Lincoln persists in treating the Dred Scott decision and local territorial jurisdiction as contradictory because his real purpose is sectional agitation! The Supreme Court determined that a Negro descended from African slaves is not a citizen under the Constitution and that Congress may not enact a Missouri Compromise exclusion. Within that framework, domestic institutions live or die by the positive enactments of local communities. Meanwhile, Mr. Lincoln preaches his 'House Divided' heresy—claiming this Union cannot endure permanently half slave and half free, inviting relentless sectional warfare between North and South until slavery is everywhere extinguished or everywhere nationalized. Our fathers framed this Union half slave and half free; why cannot it endure forever on their plan?

turns.speaker: Abraham Lincoln
turns.text: I did not say I was in favor of uniformity in all local institutions—cranberry laws, oyster laws, and road statutes differ safely across the states. Our fathers placed slavery where the public mind rested in the belief that it was in the course of ultimate extinction! They prohibited slavery in the Northwest Territory, abolished the foreign slave trade, and avoided putting the word 'slavery' in the Constitution. It is Senator Douglas, with his Nebraska Act and his doctrine of indifference—declaring he cares not whether slavery be voted down or voted up—who has dragged the nation away from the founders' course and proclaimed that slavery may spread everywhere.

turns.speaker: Thomas J. Turner
turns.text: The ninety-minute response of Senator Douglas has expired. Mr. Lincoln is now entitled to thirty minutes in closing rejoinder to address the constitutional and moral arguments raised in this debate.

turns.speaker: Abraham Lincoln
turns.text: Fellow citizens, in this closing half hour let us examine the true issue separating us. Senator Douglas tells you he cares not whether slavery is voted down or voted up, reducing the fate of human liberty in our virgin territories to a mere local police regulation and unfriendly legislation. Yet when a man contends that slavery is neither right nor wrong, he denies the central proposition of the Declaration of Independence: that all men are created equal. I have no purpose to interfere with slavery in the states where it already exists, nor to bring about social and political equality where it is unwarranted; all I am doing is refusing to say that slavery is right, and refusing to permit its spread into free federal territories.

turns.speaker: Stephen A. Douglas
turns.text: Let the people of Illinois judge between my record of constitutional Unionism and Mr. Lincoln's sectional creed. Popular sovereignty leaves every community free to shape its own police regulations and domestic institutions without congressional coercion, preserving both local self-government and the federal Union.

turns.speaker: Abraham Lincoln
turns.text: If the Freeport Doctrine means that a territorial legislature may exclude slavery despite Dred Scott, then Senator Douglas has broken with Southern Democrats who demand a federal slave code in the territories; if Dred Scott overrides local unfriendly legislation, then popular sovereignty is as thin as the soup boiled from the shadow of a pigeon that starved to death. Either way, the nation must choose whether freedom or slavery shall be the rule of our national territories. I thank you for your patient attention.

turns.speaker: Thomas J. Turner
turns.text: The joint debate at Freeport is hereby concluded. Both candidates have presented their constitutional arguments on popular sovereignty, the Dred Scott decision, and territorial slavery. The assembly is adjourned.
